claims.text: Machine learning-assisted inverse design can guide rapid discovery of refractory HEAs combining high strength, ductility, and low weight.
Machine learning surrogate modeling can efficiently navigate the large refractory-HEA compositional space.
Machine learning surrogate models can predict optimal multi-objective properties of refractory HEAs.
Multi-principal-element refractory HEA systems have a broad, largely unexplored compositional landscape.
A workflow integrating high-throughput computational screening, machine learning surrogate models, and multi-objective optimization can predict candidate refractory-HEA compositions.
Computational descriptors can be used to infer phase stability and microstructural homogeneity.
A uniform crystal lattice and minimal secondary-phase formation are indicators of microstructural homogeneity.
Machine learning models can correlate alloy composition parameters with key mechanical properties.
Fast-to-compute physical descriptors such as mixing enthalpy and atomic-size mismatch can be correlated with key mechanical properties.
Iterative optimization can identify compositions in which phase stability and microstructural homogeneity produce improved strength and ductility.
Iterative optimization can identify compositions having reduced weight relative to conventional designs.
The proposed approach will discover refractory HEAs with a balanced combination of high strength, enhanced ductility, and lower weight.
Alloys discovered by the proposed approach will outperform alloys designed solely through traditional thermo-kinetic simulations.
Traditional thermo-kinetic analysis and brute-force computational simulation are slower than the proposed workflow when exploring large compositional spaces.
Surrogate-model accuracy is limited by the composition and property ranges represented in the training data.
Predictions may be less reliable for compositions outside the training range or under untested conditions.
The success of the inverse-design approach depends on the availability and quality of training data.
Computational predictions may differ from experimentally realized alloy properties.
